title: Secretary of State Marco Rubio at the Trump Administration’s Foundry School Launch
text: hide Secretary of State Marco Rubio at the Trump Administration’s Foundry School Launch Remarks Marco Rubio, Secretary of State Donald J. Trump Institute of Peace Washington, D.C. September 3, 2026 UNDER SECRETARY HELBERG: Every so often, history hands a nation a choice: to drift, or to build. And every so often, it hands that nation a leader who inspires people to reject the drifters and build with boldness and confidence in the future. One of our guests this morning is the son of Cuban exiles, a man whose family fled a regime that confiscated everything, and who grew up understanding in his bones that freedom and prosperity are not inherited – they’re defended, and they’re built. That heritage made him clear-eyed, and it gave him something rare in Washington: the memory of what it costs when a country loses its future. For decades in the United States Senate, he warned us. He warned us that we traded our industrial base for the illusion of cheap abundance. He warned us that supply chains had become weapons pointed at us. And this year in Munich, in a speech that will be studied for a generation, he said what no Secretary of State had dared to say – that deindustrialization was a choice, and that reindustrialization must now be ours. He called on the free world not merely to defend Western civilization but to build a new Western century. Under President Trump’s leadership, he has turned that vision into policy, restoring American economic strength as the foundation of economic power, and reminding the world that the arsenal of democracy was never a metaphor – it was a factory floor. He’s a statesman, a patriot, and the driving force behind the most consequential renewal of American economic statecraft since the Second World War. Ladies and gentlemen, please join me in welcoming the 72nd Secretary of State of the United States, Secretary Marco Rubio. (Applause.) SECRETARY RUBIO: Thank you. Thank you, all of you, first of all, for being here today. Thank you – Jacob Helberg’s doing a phenomenal job. Everybody at our department is doing a great job, and I’m very proud of the work the State Department is putting in into these and other initiatives. One of the things we really wanted to do in our time here, and one of the reasons behind many of the reforms we undertook, is to allow us to have a State Department that could move at the speed of relevance, which is something we used to say all the time. Now it’s become almost a cliche, but it really is important – because world affairs are moving so quickly, economic developments are moving so quickly, and so much of that is internationalized, and it involves what we do around the world as well. And so, I’m very proud of everybody at the Department of State and all the work that they’re doing to be a part of this initiative, along with our partners in the other agencies, because this truly is an interagency challenge that we’re facing. What is the challenge that we’re here to talk about today? Let me put it to you this way: I think we made a terrible mistake in this country – not – many years ago, under people that were in charge at the time, especially at the end of the Cold War. And that was the idea that the ability to make things no longer mattered. And no matter – it didn’t matter any longer where things were made. They were to be made in the most efficient place at the lowest possible cost. That meant more profits for the company, lower costs for the consumers, and that was the way the world would work. There was this fantasy, really, that the whole world would become a free enterprise, democracies, and that everyone would look us. That ran into reality – the reality that that is not how human events have ever worked, that the nation-state still does matter, nationalism is still real, national borders still matter, and that countries are going to always act in their best interest. But the result of it is that it deindustrialized America. We lost our ability and our capacity to make things, and not just big things – not just the kinds of big machinery and things that we normally identify with industry – but even some of the most basic components that are necessary, that underpin economic life, especially in the 21st century. And we woke up to the reality just a few years ago that we are suddenly, as a nation, dangerously dependent – dangerously dependent – on other nations for all sorts of things that we need, not simply for our economic vibrancy but, in many cases, for our national security and our very survival as a prosperous nation-state. And so now we are involved in this endeavor across the board to try to reverse those mistakes. And it will be the work of multiple administrations, but it starts here and it starts now with this one that is receiving attention at its highest level. One way is just the basic ingredients that go into all this, and it’s why you’ve seen such a focus on access to not just critical minerals as raw material but also to the ability to process them. But the other is – has to be the ability to actually make things once again. And we have to understand that re-industrialization, that 21st century industrial activity is going to look different than it did in the 20th century. It’s going to involve far more skills. It’s going to involve – not just are our workers going to have to be better educated in what they’re doing, but in many cases, given the evolution and the rapidly changing dynamics of the modern world, they may have to be retrained multiple times in their career. One of the crown jewels that have powered American innovation and, ultimately, powered American economic influence and power around the world has been our system of higher education. It has produced extraordinary research; it has produced extraordinary breakthroughs. I think the sad part about it is the number of things we have innovated or created, but then they’re made somewhere else. And so, I think in the 21st century, this partnership with higher education is important, and it’s important for two reasons. First of all, why build it when – why build a new wheel when we already have a wheel? We just need to repurpose that wheel to become the place where 21st century American workers go to become empowered with the skills they need to succeed. But I also think it’s important for higher education, and we’ve got some great partners here today that are already part of this initiative, and, of course, we want this partnership to grow to include other schools as well. But I think it’s also important for higher education because, increasingly, young Americans are asking: Is the college degree worth it? Is the college route worth it? Because we have to borrow money or we have to spend money or we have to do all these sorts of things and, in the end, I get a degree, and all that degree does is either a) qualify me to get another degree or b) it may not even really lead to a job necessarily that’s different from the one I could have gotten otherwise. And I think this speaks to that, because it also – in addition to being good for our country – is an opportunity to say to students: If you come here and you go to school and you follow this curriculum, you will leave here not just with a paper credential but with the skills that make you immediately employable in a high-paying job, in a good-paying job with long-term stability. And so this partnership is critical because what I hope it means, what I hope it symbolizes – and not just symbolizes but what I hope it is evidence of – is how government partnering with non-government entities like our higher education system and the private sector, the combination of those three pillars – the private sector that needs the workers and knows what they need from the workers; the higher education system that can equip young Americans with the skills they need to fill those jobs; and government that ensures not just that it’s acting as a convening body, but ensures that our national policies reflect these priorities. These three pillars working together drive us towards this outcome that we want, and it’s very important. So, I think today is a great way to kick this off. We have great partners on board already. We hope to attract more. I want to thank all of you for being a part of it. And I – the last thing I want to say about this is that we understand that for this to work, this is not a two-year project. This is not a two-and-a-half-year project. This is a project that will involve sustainment for the long term. Multiple American administrations are going to have to make this a priority, which is why it’s so important that you see evidence that, at the highest levels of our government, now and for the future, you have that commitment. And it’s why it’s exciting for us to have the Vice President here today to speak about it, because I think the evidence is not just the importance this administration gives it, but our acknowledgement that this is an issue that’s going to require long-term and sustained attention. This has to be an endeavor that goes on beyond the next two years. It has to go on for a generation. And I think having the Vice President here today with us is evidence of that commitment. And so now I want to introduce and welcome to the stage here at the Institute of Peace, a beautiful building that the State Department’s using a lot – and we thank you all for coming – the Vice President of the United States of America, JD Vance. title: Strengthening U.S. Ties with the Pacific: Deputy Secretary Landau Engages Partners in Federated States of Micronesia, Solomon Islands, and Kiribati
text: hide Strengthening U.S. Ties with the Pacific: Deputy Secretary Landau Engages Partners in Federated States of Micronesia, Solomon Islands, and Kiribati Media Note Office of the Spokesman September 11, 2026 Fresh from his meetings with government partners at the Pacific Islands Forum in Palau, Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau traveled to the Federated States of Micronesia (FSM), Solomon Islands, and Kiribati to advance the Trump Administration’s America First economic and security priorities across the Pacific. The Deputy Secretary reaffirmed our commitment to the FSM in a bilateral meeting with FSM President Wesley Simina. The Deputy Secretary also surveyed the recovery efforts following Typhoon Sinlaku’s damage in Chuuk State where he announced the United States intends to provide over $100 million to support disaster relief and reconstruction in FSM, delivering on U.S. commitments under the Compact of Free Association. In Solomon Islands, the Deputy Secretary emphasized the bonds forged during World War II and outlined a vision for mutual progress in a free and open Pacific. He paid his respects at Guadalcanal, Red Beach, and Bloody Ridge Memorials where Americans, Solomon Islanders, and other Allied forces sacrificed their lives to turn the tide of the war. The Deputy Secretary announced U.S. support through the Ambassadors Fund for Cultural Preservation for the preservation of the Bloody Ridge battlefield as a site of perpetual remembrance and continuing education. Looking forward, he signed an agreement with Minister for Foreign Affairs and External Trade Rick Houenipwela for the Peace Corps to return to the Solomon Islands after a 26-year absence. At Honiara Airport, he concluded his visit by announcing that the U.S. Department of State, working with Congress, intends to provide four aircraft rescue and firefighting vehicles to enhance the safety of American and international tourists. He also announced the Millenium Challenge Corporation will conduct a condition assessment to determine the cost of rehabilitating the Solomon Islands Parliament. In Kiribati, the Deputy Secretary attended the Kiribati Development Partners Forum on Kiritimati Island at the invitation of President Taneti Maamau to emphasize U.S. commitment to partnership with Kiribati on economic development in line with the Kiribati 20-Year Vision. The Deputy Secretary announced the Millenium Challenge Corporation will conduct a study to update and expand the wharf on Kiritimati Island. This initiative will lay the foundation for a long-term infrastructure investment to increase access to trade and support maritime security and combatting illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing for the peoples of Kiritimati. Throughout the visit, the Deputy Secretary reaffirmed the United States’ longstanding commitment to partnering with Pacific Island nations to expand economic and commercial opportunities, strengthen digital connectivity, combat transnational criminal activity, and safeguard global health security. Meeting with senior leaders in each country, he unveiled new initiatives to advance a free and open Pacific, expand opportunities for U.S. businesses, and deliver concrete economic results for the American taxpayer. title: Restrictions on the Iranian United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) Delegation’s Movement and Acquiring Items from Wholesale Club Stores and Luxury Goods
text: hide Restrictions on the Iranian United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) Delegation’s Movement and Acquiring Items from Wholesale Club Stores and Luxury Goods Press Statement Thomas "Tommy" Pigott, Principal Deputy Spokesperson September 22, 2025 The United States took action this week to impose maximum pressure on the Iranian regime by restricting their UNGA delegation’s movement and access to wholesale club stores and luxury goods. We will not allow the Iranian regime to allow its clerical elites to have a shopping spree in New York while the Iranian people endure poverty, crumbling infrastructure, and dire shortages of water and electricity. Secretary Rubio is also restricting the Iranian delegation to the areas strictly necessary to transit to and from the UN headquarters district to conduct their official UN business. The security of Americans is always our priority, and the United States will not allow the Iranian regime to use UNGA as an excuse to travel freely in New York to promote its terrorist agenda. By preventing Iranian regime officials from exploiting diplomatic travel to the UN as a means to obtain goods unavailable to the Iranian public, we are sending a clear message: When the United States says it stands with the people of Iran, we mean it. Today’s actions affirm the United States’ unwavering commitment to supporting the Iranian people in their pursuit of accountability for the regime and for a better life. title: Joint Statement on Sudan: Political Track
text: hide Joint Statement on Sudan: Political Track Media Note Office of the Spokesman June 8, 2026 The text of the following statement was released by the Governments of the United States of America and the countries and organizations of Belgium, France, Germany, Greece, Italy, Norway, the United Kingdom, African Union (AU), the European Union (EU), the Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD), the League of Arab States (LAS), and the United Nations (UN) on the occasion of the conclusion of the Quintet (AU, IGAD, LAS, EU, and UN) consultations with Sudanese political stakeholders in Addis Ababa from June 3-5, 2026 following up on the Sudan conference in Berlin of April 15, 2026. Begin Text Belgium, France, Germany, Greece, Italy, Norway, the United Kingdom, the United States, the African Union (AU), the European Union (EU), the Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD), the League of Arab States (LAS), and the United Nations (UN) reaffirm their shared and unwavering commitment to the people of Sudan and to a peaceful, democratic, and stable future for the country, as well as to the sovereignty, unity, and territorial integrity of Sudan. We express deep concern over the devastating humanitarian consequences of the ongoing conflict, where millions face displacement, acute food insecurity, and limited access to basic services, while attacks on civilians and infrastructure persist. The protection of civilians must remain central. We reaffirm the urgent need for a humanitarian truce, leading to a permanent ceasefire. We welcome the outcomes of the Berlin Conference, including the ‘Berlin Principles for Sudan’ adopted by 22 countries and organizations and the ‘Joint Call to End the War and Advance a Sudanese-Owned Political Process’ issued by Sudanese civilian stakeholders and facilitated by the Quintet (the African Union, the Intergovernmental Authority on Development, League of Arab States, European Union, and the United Nations). Together, they serve as an important step towards strengthening international coordination and reinforcing support for a civilian-led path towards a durable peaceful settlement. We stand united in our belief that there can be no military solution to this crisis, and that a sustainable resolution must be rooted in an inclusive, civilian-led political process that reflects the aspirations of the Sudanese people. We underscore the importance of advancing the civilian track as a central pillar in efforts to end the war and lay the groundwork for a democratic and inclusive civilian-led transition process that is free of control or undue influence by any one party and that is independent of extremist groups. We support a swift and time-bound civilian track that leads to a civilian-led transition, with an intention to continue to review and assess progress and implementation of agreed benchmarks. Appropriate measures will be considered by the international community against those who seek to undermine the civilian transition process. We reaffirm that Sudan’s future governance is for the Sudanese people to decide through an independent, inclusive, and transparent civilian-led transition process. To this end, we collectively support the Quintet’s urgent preparations and commencement—in the coming few weeks—of a comprehensive and inclusive Sudanese civilian-led dialogue process. This process, and its preparations, should bring together a broad spectrum of Sudanese civilian and political actors, including representatives of civil society, women’s groups, youth, and stakeholders representing Sudan’s geographic and social diversity, and should be conducted in a manner that is transparent, credible, and free from coercion. We further express our readiness to support the Quintet’s efforts to ensure that this dialogue is structured in a way that enables it to be feasibly and reasonably concluded in a timely manner—ideally within six months—and to complement efforts for peace and the broader transition. Its outcome should establish a clear pathway toward a transition process to an independent civilian-led government, grounded in legitimacy, accountability, and respect for human rights. We underscore that the establishment of such an independent civilian-led government is indispensable to ensuring a durable end to the conflict. We call for broader international support and reaffirm our commitment to continued coordination to help end the conflict, alleviate suffering, and support Sudan’s peaceful transition, as well as ensuring mutually reinforcing action in support of advancing these ends goals. End Text Tags African Union Belgium Bureau of African Affairs Bureau of Democracy, Human Rights, and Labor Bureau of European and Eurasian Affairs Bureau of International Organizations Conflicts and Peacekeeping European Union (EU) France Germany Greece Human Rights Humanitarian Diplomacy Italy Norway Office of the Spokesman Sudan United Kingdom United Nations (UN)

title: Secretary of State Marco Rubio Remarks to the Press
text: hide Secretary of State Marco Rubio Remarks to the Press Remarks Marco Rubio, Secretary of State Philippine International Convention Center Manila, Philippines July 22, 2026 SECRETARY RUBIO: Okay. I want to get you guys some stuff. So you ready? Go ahead, go. QUESTION: Mr. Secretary, you had quite a long meeting here with — SECRETARY RUBIO: Yeah. QUESTION: — your Chinese counterpart. QUESTION: That’s okay. It went quite long. Is that — SECRETARY RUBIO: Yeah. QUESTION: Does that give the impression that the meeting was tense? And can you give us a sense of what you talked about? SECRETARY RUBIO: No, we have to translate; translations always take longer, the back and forth. QUESTION: Yeah. And give us a sense of what you talked about. SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, we talked a lot about the visit in September, and that was really the gist of it. It was just to create the groundwork for another positive visit. I think President Xi will have a very positive visit when he comes to Washington. Look, these are the two most powerful countries in the world, particularly economics, but also – I mean, we have to have a relationship. And obviously, there are areas of great differences. Both sides will acknowledge that. We’ll have to work through those. And I think these differences will exist for the foreseeable future, and our job is to sort of manage those so that they never get out of control. We’re, obviously, always going to defend our national interest. And I expect they’ll do the same, as they define it. But I think there are some areas of potential cooperation. So the work we need to do between now and September is to identify what those areas are so that we can lay the groundwork for a very positive visit to Washington, and – in September. And so we talked a lot about that. QUESTION: Was there disagreement on election interference? SECRETARY RUBIO: We didn’t discuss that topic. QUESTION: Mr. Secretary, are China and Russia giving targeting information to Iran? These last few attacks have been very devastating to U.S. troops. SECRETARY RUBIO: Look, all I would say is that anytime you’re in a combat zone like that, there’s danger associated with it. I mean, at the end, this actually proves the point that this is what Iran has been investing its money in for the last 20 years. QUESTION: But are China and Russia giving targeting information to them? SECRETARY RUBIO: I’m not going to discuss that, other than to say that nothing that’s happened – no – nothing that China has done has in any way changed the trajectory of the – of what you’re seeing in terms of the conflicts we’re having with Iran. And in fact, in some cases, they’ve actually been quite cooperative — QUESTION: In what way? SECRETARY RUBIO: — in regards to what they potentially could have done but didn’t do. I think the Chinese – and I’ll let them tell you, but I don’t think they’re big fans of what Iran is trying to do in the straits. In fact, they’ve said so publicly, that they oppose tolling or any sort of restraint on freedom of navigation in the straits. And we hope they’ll continue to say that, and it’s important that other countries say that as well. QUESTION: President Trump was asked a similar question, and I’d like to pose it to you. Is the U.S. strategy to strike Iran into submission? And why do you think Iran is not giving in right now after they — SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, look, the United States is – Iran’s in a lot of trouble. I mean, any day I – they obviously don’t have a free press that reports on the – for example, you guys will report on the impact it’s having on the U.S. economy and gas prices and this and that; they don’t have that in Iran. But I can tell you they’re facing hyperinflation, runaway inflation, high food costs. These were all pre-existing. They’ve all gotten worse. They’ve suffered a tremendous amount of damage to their military infrastructure, but they’ve also spent 20 years taking every penny they have and not spending it on their country. They spent it on sponsoring terrorist groups and building up their missiles and their drone systems. And this is the – what you’re seeing them use now, which is greatly diminished, is exactly the conventional shield that they were going to hide behind to pursue a nuclear program and challenge the world to do anything about it or face the wrath of what they were doing. A year from now, Iran would have had so many missiles and drones that they would have been behind a conventional shield that would have given them immunity to do whatever they wanted. So right now, however, I can just say here’s what’s happening. It’s pretty straightforward. Ships are trying to go through the straits, and they’re getting blown up. Commercial ships are going through the straits, and they’re being blown up. The United States is defending that shipping and, in addition, is targeting the places that are launching against those ships to continue to degrade Iran’s ability to target and harm global shipping. So that’s what’s happening here, and that’s what we’re focused on. QUESTION: Mr. Secretary — QUESTION: You mentioned this morning that Iran isn’t keeping its commitments. So even if a MOU is revived, what can be done to yield different results? SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, look, all these things are compliance-based, right? I mean, if you make a deal, if you sign onto an agreement and then you violate the agreement, the agreement’s no longer valid. That doesn’t mean you can’t have a future agreement, but ultimately, that future agreement will have to be judged on whether or not you’re complying with the conditions. And that deal called for the opening of the straits, free and fair navigation. In fact, they were supposed to put out a statement to that regard a week and a half ago. And instead, on the day they were supposed to put out that statement, instead of doing that, they targeted and blew up or hit a ship. So we remain open to diplomacy. We remain open to working it out in a negotiated way. But right now, they don’t seem to be serious about that. And so we’re going to continue to protect shipping. We think other countries should join us in that endeavor. We don’t need them to, but they should, because they’re more impacted by it than we are. And at the same time, we are going to, when the opportunity presents itself, degrade their ability to target global shipping. QUESTION: China’s been sending its coast guard in — SECRETARY RUBIO: What now? QUESTION: China has been sending its coast guard in toward Taiwan, doing patrols near Taiwan. I know the U.S. has said this has been destabilizing. Did you raise that with Wang Yi? SECRETARY RUBIO: It always comes up in every one of our meetings because we obviously disagree with those actions. And we actually think that they run contrary to the spirit of what we’re trying to work out with them with regards to strategic stability. But the bigger point to make in that regard is that the U.S. will continue to – we’re never going to accept that international waterways are somehow under the control of other countries. We’ll continue to sail through international waterways and freedom of navigation efforts of that kind, and we’ll continue to live up to our commitments – for example, with the Philippines and other countries – in terms of the treaty commitments that we have. And again, it speaks to areas of disagreement when it comes to our policies with China. Those need to be managed very carefully because obviously a conflict, be it economic or otherwise, between the U.S. and China would have a dramatic global impact. So the difficult job of geopolitics and foreign policy is managing your differences and not doing anything that runs contrary to our national interests, but at the same time trying to avoid conflict that could lead to something really catastrophic for the world. And I think we have an obligation to do that, which is why it’s important for us to continue to talk to China, irrespective of our differences. It’s important to – if you go back to the height of the Cold War, even in the height of the Cold War, even in its most tense moments, the United States and the Soviet Union were – communicated, at least at a military-to-military level and even at a diplomatic level, and in many ways that prevented catastrophe. So I’m not saying we’re at that stage with China, but what I am saying is it would, frankly, be reckless and irresponsible for the U.S. and China not to have a relationship, given the impact and the – our countries have on the global economy and on the world. QUESTION: Did you discuss with China, with Minister Wang Yi, the working group, or any more details of the Board of Trade, Board of Investment, any of these other ideas? SECRETARY RUBIO: Yes, we did. We did, and we’re moving towards implementation of that, and I think that’s one of the potential concrete deliverables that we can have before September when that visit happens. And again, those are good ideas, and they come in the aftermath of the visit we took to China earlier this year. And so we did discuss that, yes. QUESTION: Has the U.S. — QUESTION: Russia’s Lavrov revealed that he’s going to be meeting with you tomorrow. SECRETARY RUBIO: Yeah. QUESTION: If that happens, are you going to press him on Ukraine, or are you simply keeping — SECRETARY RUBIO: No, we’re going to – I don’t know if the term is “press him.” We’re going to talk about it. Obviously, the war in Ukraine, I think, has in many ways impeded the ability of Russia and the United States to find areas of agreement on other topics. That doesn’t mean we won’t seek to find other areas of potential cooperation. But by the same token, we’d like to see that war come to an end. We think it would be good for Russia if that war came to an end. So we’ll raise it. And as I said, the U.S. remains open and willing to play a constructive role in bringing that war to an end, if that opportunity presents itself. And it might. We’re open to it, to playing that role, because we think right now – and I think the Russians would agree – we’re probably the only country in the world that can play that role in that, in trying to bring that to an end. QUESTION: What kind of role is the U.S. playing right now in doing that? I mean, there’s still some kind of quiet talks going on or outreach by — SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, I think that you’ve seen it kind of fall off a little bit over the last few months. Perhaps there are now new conditions in place that will allow that conversation to happen. It’s one of the things we’ll explore tomorrow in our conversation. I saw the Foreign Minister Lavrov last night briefly. We didn’t talk about any of this, but I saw him last night when he arrived at the opening dinner. And we’ll talk more tomorrow. Obviously, to be fair to you guys, I mean, a lot of the stuff I’ll talk to him about, I’m not going to, like, put in a press release because it undermines the ability to find understandings. But we’ll talk about it and see if there’s an opening now or an opportunity for us to play a constructive role. But there are other areas that the U.S. and Russia can cooperate on that we – again, going back to the point I made about China. This is very simple. Russia possesses the – we are the two largest nuclear-armed countries on the planet. For us not to talk would be reckless and irresponsible. We have to have a relationship with the Russian Government, even though we have areas of disagreement, and in the case of Ukraine, perhaps an opportunity to – if we can play a constructive role to bring it to an end. So I’m sure that’ll come up tomorrow; there’s no doubt. But we’ll talk about some other stuff too. QUESTION: Mr. Secretary — QUESTION: But The Wall Street Journal is reporting that President Trump has approved a nuclear deal with Saudi Arabia. Do you have any details on that? SECRETARY RUBIO: Yeah, I’m – I’ll let the White House officials sort of put out an official statement about anything with regards to that. But I saw the same reporting this morning. But let me let that go through the – I don’t – I’d prefer it be put out; when there is something to say, that we will say it through official channels. QUESTION: Can you confirm that? QUESTION: Has the U.S. asked South Korea or their Asian allies to contribute naval assets or something? SECRETARY RUBIO: We didn’t ask them that today. Look, I think it’s to their benefit, right? If you look at the region, they heavily depend on oil and natural gas that comes from this part of the world. Now, one of the interesting things you’ve seen is that the supplies that are reaching many of the countries in the region have begun to change. They’re buying more LNG from us than ever before. They’re also buying more oil from us than ever before. So I think some of the changes you have seen and where people are getting their energy are going to be permanent after what you’ve seen here. But nonetheless, the straits remain an important source of energy for many of the countries in this region. It’s about 20 percent of the global oil that’s purchased. So I think we would – we think it would be to their benefit to participate in an effort. QUESTION: But you didn’t make that ask today in these conversations? SECRETARY RUBIO: We didn’t ask directly today, but we’ve had those conversations with them in the past. Every country has different restrictions on what they need to do in order to authorize that. Some have to get legislative approval. Some can do it unilaterally. Every country’s different. But we’ve certainly raised it with different countries. We don’t need them to do it, but we think it would be beneficial if they did. And some of these countries have unique capabilities in terms of mine clearing and things of that nature. So it’d be great if they joined the effort, and I think some of them may eventually do so. It’s in their interest to do so. But we didn’t reach any agreement on that today. Frankly, it wasn’t the cornerstone of what our conversations were about. QUESTION: Mr. Secretary, a lot of the ASEAN countries have expressed how terrible the war in Iran is for them when it comes to economically and the energy crunch. But Israel’s finance minister sort of struck a tone in a different direction, said that the tit-for-tat is actually the best possible situation for Israel because it’s weakening Iran. Does this show that there are some differences between the United States and Israel when it comes to how they view this war? The United States is trying to end this. For the Israelis, the hostility is continuing. Is it their benefit? SECRETARY RUBIO: Yeah, look, I can’t comment on what some one individual in government said in Israel. I can just generally tell you that, by and large, we think that a nuclear-armed Iran is an unacceptable thing. It can’t happen. And that’s what they were going to do, if they hid behind this conventional shield that they were building. And the President just wasn’t going to stand by and allow that to happen. Within two years, Iran could say: We’re breaking out to a nuclear weapon; you can’t do anything about it or we’re going to overwhelm you with tens of thousands of drones and missiles, which they were on pace to build. They can’t do that now. That’s certainly weakened them. As far as the impact it’s had on the global economy, I mean, Iran is targeting global shipping in an international waterway and demanding to control which ships can go and which ones cannot. That just is unacceptable. We’re not going to accept that. We’re not going to allow that to be the status quo. But ultimately, there are other countries that should feel just as strongly as we do, because they’re actually more impacted by it than we are. QUESTION: Did you discuss with Minister Jaishankar – did he raise at all any concern by India about the tariffs announced by the President on generic drug makers? A lot of Americans buy their generic drugs from Indian companies that import. Is that something that came up in your discussions at all? SECRETARY RUBIO: I mean, not with me. I mean, we didn’t get into depth on pharmaceuticals today, obviously. I would expect them to be concerned about it, but they didn’t raise it today. But they might have with others in our system, because we obviously deal with the Indians; we’re very close to them. So — QUESTION: Mr. Secretary, you and the President have been very blunt in your anti-communist language recently. You put out that recent report on Cuba. Don’t you think it’s inconsistent in that you haven’t addressed the same issues with China? They’re the largest communist party in the world, 100 million. SECRETARY RUBIO: Yeah, but our issue is with communist interference inside of our country. That report was about what these different elements do to interfere in our country and to undermine our foreign policy. QUESTION: But the President recently talked about China’s election interference in the U.S., and as we know, there are many other ways in which China has influence within the U.S. SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, again, what the President put out on Thursday that was a declassification of documents from our Intelligence Community – that’s what he put out. He declassified intelligence assessments from our Intelligence Community. But your question was about communist influence. Yeah, the United States doesn’t want to be a communist country. We’re never going to be a communist country, and we’re not going to allow communist influences to undermine our politics or our society. So I don’t know what the inconsistency you’re referring to is. It’s very clear. Obviously, we understand the Chinese system and other systems. But I can tell you our system doesn’t want communism, and we’re certainly not going to allow communist efforts to undermine American society and drive wedges into our country. And that’s what we’re seeing. And by the way, one of the leading culprits of that for many years, the intellectual authors have been, particularly in our hemisphere, is the Cuban regime, which our report on Monday outlined. QUESTION: Are the Cubans having a bigger impact than the Chinese? QUESTION: Mr. Secretary, did you express concern regarding the clash between China and the Philippines in the South China Sea? SECRETARY RUBIO: Did we discuss it with — QUESTION: Clash between China and the Philippines in the South China Sea. SECRETARY RUBIO: Oh, yeah, it’s been a high-profile issue. We’ve all seen it. And it’s sort of an escalatory thing that we think is very negative and benefits no one. And obviously, we’ve reiterated in every meeting we’ve had that the U.S. has a treaty arrangement with the Philippines. I believe we’re the only treaty partner the Philippines has. We intend to live up to our treaty obligations, and I think we’ve done so, and we’ll continue to do so. QUESTION: Secretary, the question — QUESTION: With scenes of escalation, how difficult is it to inspire confidence at these meetings, such as the ones you’ve had today, that the U.S. can bring an end, a quick end, to the war in Iran? SECRETARY RUBIO: I’m sorry, what was the — QUESTION: Is it difficult to inspire confidence that the U.S. can swiftly and effectively end the war in Iran at these meetings? SECRETARY RUBIO: No, I think everybody here understands that the U.S. would love to reach a diplomatic settlement. We would love to reach an agreement if it were possible with Iran that would ensure they never have a nuclear weapon and obviously help stop them. And we’d love to have an agreement where they say we’ll no longer sponsor terrorism and we will not pursue a nuclear weapon or the things you need for a nuclear weapon. I think if there’s a lack of confidence, it’s the lack of confidence that the Iranian regime will ever agree to any of those things. That would be the lack of confidence. And the bigger lack of confidence should be that they’ve already made commitments very recently in a memorandum of understanding, and within two weeks they’d violated it. So I think if there’s any undermining of confidence, it’s confidence that the Iranian system as it currently is structured can reach an agreement. So you wonder whether they’re serious about an agreement in the short term. But look, we always – the President always prefers to negotiate and reach a deal on these things. And we’re prepared – willing to do that. We’ve tried to do that now for a year and a half, but we’re also not going to sit by and let ships be blown up or Americans be attacked. QUESTION: Is there hope for a compromise? QUESTION: If Iran refuses to negotiate seriously — SECRETARY RUBIO: Who is this? QUESTION: If Iran refuses to negotiate seriously — SECRETARY RUBIO: Iran, yeah? QUESTION: — what is the next step? More sanctions, more military actions? Are you prepared for long-term confrontation, all right? SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, the President has many options available to him if they continue to insist on not being cooperative, and I won’t get ahead of the President on any of those. But I think Iran knows we have many options as well. QUESTION: The President suggested that – give me a second – the President suggested that Iran should be added to Russia sanctions act. Is this kind of acknowledgment of Moscow-Tehran growing alliance? SECRETARY RUBIO: Of what now? QUESTION: I guess acknowledging this growing alliance between the two, because you’re adding – suggesting to add Iran to Russia sanctions act? SECRETARY RUBIO: Oh, I just think the President views as a legislative vehicle that’s going to pass in Congress and provides him more authorities to impose higher economic costs on Iran if it’s necessary to do so. So I don’t think it has – I don’t – I think it’s just a bill that’s moving, and it’s a sanctions bill, and so it makes sense if you’re going to add additional sanctions to do it to that bill. QUESTION: On Cuba, is the goal still creating regime change through economic collapse, or is the military option still on the table? SECRETARY RUBIO: I think the goal is to have a Cuba where the people of Cuba can experience prosperity, safety, security, and a better life moving forward, the way Cubans are able to do all over the world when they leave Cuba. And we’re prepared to be very realistic about how you do that, and patient about how – you got a serious process that leads to that. And we’ve engaged them from time to time in that regard, and they know where we stand on that issue, and hopefully that’s where it arrives. The fundamental Cuba – the fundamental problem Cuba has right now is two things. Number one is their economic system doesn’t work because it – that economic system doesn’t exist anywhere else in the world. It’s completely backwards; it just doesn’t work. And that’s why people have to leave that country. And number two, it’s they’re no longer getting free oil from Venezuela. That’s their biggest problem. They’re not getting free oil from Venezuela – which, by the way, they weren’t using for their power grid. They were taking about 60 percent of the free oil they were getting from Venezuela and reselling it for cash. So the biggest problem Cuba has is that the regime is a disaster, their economic model doesn’t work, and the people who run the country don’t know what the hell they’re doing. And all they’re most interested in is holding onto power. They are afraid of economic prosperity because they are afraid that economic prosperity and economic liberties will – they will lose control over people. And that’s always been the struggle they’ve faced in recent times. But again, look, we’ve been – just today we began shipping over $100 million of humanitarian assistance to Cuba which will be distributed by nongovernmental entities on the ground. So it – we’ll – we’re willing to engage with them; we’ve engaged with them in the past. We’ll keep talking to them about the kind of changes they can make. But this is 90 miles from our shores. This is a government that has spent – a regime that has spent the better part of 30, 40, 50 years destabilizing the region in the movements that they’ve supported, and they’ve lost, I don’t know, 10 to 15 percent of their population since 2021 because of how mismanaged the country is. We want it to have a better future, and we’re prepared to do things that help them get there. But they have to decide they want to do that. The people that are in charge there right now just don’t want to do it. QUESTION: Several people in your administration were talking about how they expected the – just to follow up – to see regime change or to see big changes in Cuba – economic, political – by the end of this year. That’s what a lot of them were saying consistently. SECRETARY RUBIO: Who’s “a lot of them?” Who was saying that? QUESTION: People within the administration who work on this issue. They weren’t — SECRETARY RUBIO: Like who? Because I work on this issue more than anybody else, and I never said that. QUESTION: They weren’t predicting it, but, like, there was an expectation that Cuba was so weak that it was going to happen. SECRETARY RUBIO: No, look, guys, I mean, you – look, this – global affairs are not like – we’re not a miniseries, like, you get in three episodes and it’s over. I mean, global affairs are difficult. You’re talking about a system that’s been in place since 1959. You talk about a country that’s suffered tremendously because of poor leadership and a bad economic model. You’re talking about a regime that’s survived all these years because they had a foreign sponsor, be it the Soviet Union or Hugo Chávez. They don’t have that anymore. So it’s – these are complex things that take time, and obviously we’re prepared to do what we can do to effectuate a positive change in Cuba because it directly impacts our national security. Cuba matters to us because it’s 90 miles from our shores, and it has a direct impact on our national security – be it the things they’ve been involved in in the past, the countries they’ve aligned with in the past and currently, or the threat of mass migration, which is always a risk that you run when countries are as deeply destabilized as Cuba. It’s a failed state. It’s a failed state. But I’ve never laid out any timeline as to what change would look like or when it would happen. I wish it was tomorrow because they deserve it; the people of Cuba deserve a better future. QUESTION: You mentioned — QUESTION: Mr. Secretary, on your argument that Iran has violated the MOU, isn’t the MOU inherently flawed because of paragraph five that explicitly acknowledges Iran has power in the Strait of Hormuz, whereas no other formal agreement before had acknowledged or recognized that? SECRETARY RUBIO: No, I don’t think that’s what the MOU says, and it’s not the way we interpreted it from the very beginning. We understood that to mean — QUESTION: But isn’t that the — SECRETARY RUBIO: No, we understood that to mean that they would ensure that no ships were being blown up, and they chose to violate that. The MOU does not give them the right to launch drones and missiles against commercial shipping vessels. The MOU doesn’t give them a right to do that. And they chose do it. QUESTION: But why acknowledge their power over the strait to begin with? SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, we don’t acknowledge their power, but – the only thing I’d tell you, that — QUESTION: Or some authority. SECRETARY RUBIO: No. They have missiles and drones and they’re launching them against ships. The MOU doesn’t say you’re allowed to launch missiles and drones against commercial shipping in the Straits of Hormuz. It doesn’t say that anywhere in the MOU. QUESTION: You said that – you mentioned, Secretary, that China has been cooperative in some ways with the issue of Iran. What were you — SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, I’m not going to tell you about all of them, but I’m going to tell you one in particular, and that is they’ve been pretty clear that they don’t support any tolling or restrictions on global shipping through an international waterway. And a statement like that from a country like China is important. QUESTION: President Trump — QUESTION: How concerning is the Houthi threat for the additional shipments of energy from the Saudis? Are you worried that that could have a — SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, the Houthis have done that in the past, as you know. They’ve threatened global shipping there in the past. And again, anything that restricts shipping through the Red Sea would be problematic, for the same reasons that the Strait of Hormuz is problematic. So we’re watching that closely, that situation. We’ve been engaging the Saudis on – a number of times over the last week in regards to that threat. It’s not a new threat, but it – it’s one that’s manifested itself in the past. But at the gist of that issue is the fact that, again, Iran is in the middle of it. Talk about the troublemaker in the region – it’s Iran. They chose – they decided to send direct flights from Tehran into Yemen carrying IRGC elements and others into the country, and the Saudis responded to it. And that’s what led to the situation we’re now facing. But we hope it can be de-escalated. Obviously, we’re not particularly close to the Houthis in terms of being able to influence the decisions they make. But I think it’s just another example – the Houthis, Hizballah, the militias in Iraq, Hamas – this is what Iran spends its money on, this – not on its people. It’s on supporting terrorist organizations and destabilizing actors in the region. QUESTION: You’ve mentioned a couple times that — QUESTION: Are you satisfied with what China’s — QUESTION: — other countries should join the U.S. to protect shipping in the strait. Have you gotten any offers? SECRETARY RUBIO: Yeah, because it’s their shipping. QUESTION: Have you gotten any offers? SECRETARY RUBIO: Yeah, we’ve had conversations. There are countries that have expressed interest. Again, some of them have different ways they have to get there in terms of how it’s authorized. Some need an international flag; they need to do it under the mandate of an international organization. Some need to go through the legislative process. But the reason why I mentioned it to you is because if you look at where that oil and you look at where that energy is destined, it’s not to the United States. It’s to other countries. And so – plus I think every country in the world has an interest in protecting the right of shipping in international waters and freedom of navigation. QUESTION: I know you said you didn’t want to get into the details on the Saudi civilian nuclear agreement, but just broadly, for people who have nonproliferation concerns, for people who listen to U.S. rhetoric about how dangerous it would be for another country to get a nuclear weapon, doesn’t having a less-than-gold-standard agreement in the Middle East run a risk? SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, I’m not going to opine directly on that agreement. We’re going to put out – if and when the moment is appropriate, we’ll put out that in writing. We have to do it with Congress anyways, so we’ll certainly do it publicly. But suffice it to say the U.S. is not going to reach any agreement with any country in the world that leads to the risk of proliferation. QUESTION: Did you discuss nonproliferation in the meeting with the Chinese or will you be bringing that up with Mr. Lavrov tomorrow? SECRETARY RUBIO: On nuclear? QUESTION: Yeah. Just – the President stopped at restarting talks. SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, we didn’t talk about it this time. We’ve talked about it in the past, and I think the President’s point – and he’s right – is in the modern era, if we’re going to have a nuclear arms restriction talks and arms control talks, it has to include the Chinese side, because they’re rapidly building their own nuclear capabilities. I would imagine the Chinese will argue that once they catch up to the U.S. and Russia, then they’ll enter these negotiations, but until then – I think that’s been their historic argument in the past, but I think the President rightly points out that in the 21st century, if you’re going to have true arms control, it has to be triparty. It has to be the U.S., Russia, but also China. But we didn’t discuss it today. QUESTION: Are you satisfied with what China’s been doing on the fentanyl issue? It was the basis for a lot of tariffs that appear to be – they keep getting struck down — SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, we continue to talk to them about that issue, and, obviously, I think we’ve made some progress. They’ve – some of the commitments that they made in – earlier this year, they’ve begun to live by. Others are – remain a work in progress. And I know that as recently as today, our law enforcement is visiting China, and we’ve had their law enforcement come to Washington earlier in the year. So we remain engaged with them, and ultimately, we think in the long term this poses a threat to China as well, so I would hope that they would have an interest in being cooperative. Because in the end, these same elements that are shipping fentanyl precursors all over the world will eventually do the same, if they’re not doing it already, inside of China and their neighboring countries. So it’s a work in progress, but I think we’ve made some progress on that front, but not entirely where we need to be. QUESTION: Mr. Secretary, after — QUESTION: Earlier you met with Japanese foreign minister. SECRETARY RUBIO: Yes. QUESTION: China has (inaudible) its economic and military pressure on Japan. So how do you see the worsening of Japan-China relationship? How do see the – how do you view the worsening Japan-China — SECRETARY RUBIO: Oh, the worsening. Yeah. Yeah. So look, I mean, obviously, we’re very close to Japan. We understand what they’re facing right now. They’re facing real restrictions, export controls and all sorts of things. And obviously, we talked about some of the aggressive measures that have been taken. It’s a troubling trend. I don’t think that China-Japan relations are at their high point right now. We’re very close to Japan. We have treaty obligations with Japan. We have a deep history of cooperation with Japan, and that’s going to continue. But we see it. We’re concerned. QUESTION: Mr. Secretary, after release – after securing one American’s release from Iran last week, should Americans expect more detainees to come home, including our colleague Reza Valizadeh? SECRETARY RUBIO: I think they should all be home. I can’t – I’m not going to predict or prognosticate what others we may see released, but we would like to see them all – all the wrongfully detained people released, not just from Iran but all over the world. But it’ll always be a priority in our conversations if and when those restart. QUESTION: When are they — QUESTION: How is that channel working? There’s so much hostilities literally between Iran and the United States, yet you were able to — SECRETARY RUBIO: Which channel? QUESTION: The channel to get wrongfully detained people out obviously just bore some success. How is that happening amidst this warfare going on? SECRETARY RUBIO: Yeah. I mean, look, I think that’s a valid point. It – we were fortunate to see one instance in which one person who shouldn’t have been there was – should not have been held there was released. We’d like to see more. It’s a feature of our conversation with them. It would obviously be easier to have that conversation if some of these other things weren’t ongoing. But I think the fact they were even detained to begin with speaks volumes as to the nature of the regime that we’re dealing with. But – yeah, I mean, it’s not the most productive moment for it, but we’re very fortunate and blessed that that lady got out, because she never should have been held in the first place. QUESTION: Mr. Secretary, is there anything you can tell you about the pending U.S. arms sale to Taiwan? SECRETARY RUBIO: About – I’m sorry? Well, there was one late last year, and the other one continues to be under review. As I said, we had the largest single sale ever in December, so it’s not like nothing has happened. But since – there’s a second pending sale that’s been notified to Congress, but it’s still undergoing a review internally. QUESTION: But why – why is it under review? Your State Department sent it to Congress; Congress approved it informally. SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, there’s a lot of reasons. I know, but there’s a lot of reasons why arms are under review, and that includes we have to look at our own stockpiles, we have to look at the availability of whatever it is we’re promising to do; as you know, there’s a huge effort on our part to restart our defense industrial base and restart its ability to produce – people ask this all the time. I mean, we’ve made very extensive sales and continue to make sales – for example, to Ukraine – and before that they were actually – we gave them to Ukraine. So all these things have an impact, and we do have our own domestic needs that have to be balanced with whatever commitments we make to other countries. So it would be normal for a large sale to be reviewed in that context. QUESTION: Is the U.S. trying to get — QUESTION: One of the Tate brothers’ lawyers mentioned you by name. I know — SECRETARY RUBIO: Who? QUESTION: One of the Tate brothers’ lawyers mentioned you by name. Do you have a plan to get involved with the extradition challenge that they have been appealing? SECRETARY RUBIO: Mentioned me by name? QUESTION: Yes. Yeah. SECRETARY RUBIO: Oh. No, look, that – extraditions, I don’t know the details of this particular case. I’ve been overseas, but I mean, I know who you’re talking about. QUESTION: Yeah. SECRETARY RUBIO: I just don’t know the details of it. These cases have a process that they go through in the courts. My understanding is that they’re involved in that judicial process. And so that’ll play itself out at this point. And – but there’s no role for us to play at this moment or maybe ever in that regard. But it – I’m not going to opine on something that’s still working through a legal process. QUESTION: Is the U.S. trying to get Syria involved in fighting Hizballah? QUESTION: Can you tell us a little bit about your strategy for the National Security Council? SECRETARY RUBIO: Hold on. Go ahead. QUESTION: Is the U.S. trying to get Syria involved in fighting Hizballah, as the President has suggested? SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, the Syrian authorities are not big fans of Hizballah. But what we’ve encouraged Syria to do is to focus on its own internal challenges that it has in sort of building a nation-state. They still face pretty substantial challenges and threats from within. I mean, ISIS remains a threat there. There are other areas of cooperation. As you know, we’ve removed them from the list of State Sponsors of Terrorism, which we hope will lead to the sort of economic revival that the country desperately needs. Syria is a country that has a history of different communities for many, many years living alongside one another in peace – Sunni, Shia, Christian – I mean, it’s a country – Kurds. And – but they have a huge project on their hands in that regard, and so we’ve encouraged them to focus on that. But we understand the threat that Hizballah – I mean, Hizballah is an enemy of this new government in Syria, and they in many ways have sought to – will seek to undermine that government over time. And one of the best things Syria can do to secure its future is to secure their border with Lebanon so that we don’t have weapons and arms coming back and forth across that border in an effort to destabilize Syria. What were you asking? QUESTION: Mr. Secretary, many national security advisors have put their stamp on the NSC bureaucracy – Scowcroft model; big, large models during the Obama administration. How do you want to be remembered for the stamp that you’re putting on this? Are you streamlining things — SECRETARY RUBIO: The NSC works for the President. And so the stamp we want to have is the stamp any NSC director should have. It’s not my stamp. The NSC is there to serve the President. And each president will have different requirements for what they want the NSC’s role to be. And so to the extent I want a legacy with regards to the NSC, it is an NSC that was responsive to the needs of this particular administration and this President’s style of leadership. He’s very hands-on, he’s very involved, and our job at the NSC is to coordinate the interagency to execute on the President’s policies. And that’s how I view the NSC. That’s the way it should always be. QUESTION: Does it still have its convening power — SECRETARY RUBIO: Sure, it happens every day. QUESTION: — or has it been depopulated so much that other agencies are starting to — SECRETARY RUBIO: I think the NSC was way too large to begin with – 400, 300 people. We don’t need 300 people in the NSC to coordinate the interagency. That’s why you have career people and others at the State Department, and at Treasury, and at Energy, and at the Department of War, and the intelligence agencies. And the job of the NSC is to coordinate the interagency so that it’s executing on the President’s foreign policy and developing options through the interagency. So the expertise should reside in the different agencies of government now. And the NSC’s job is simply to be the coordinator of that effort, to deliver on the President’s intent – either to present the President options, or to execute on the President’s directive. That’s what the NSC is doing, and I think, quite successfully. You don’t need a large bureaucracy to do that. QUESTION: There are Americans in China that have been wrongfully detained, Chen Youlin and Min Zin. SECRETARY RUBIO: Yeah. QUESTION: Did you raise those today? I mean — SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, we always raise the case of Americans, and we do so outside of these meetings as well. We do so through the embassy; we do it through multiple engagements. QUESTION: Do you expect that China should release them ahead of or as part of the meeting? SECRETARY RUBIO: We want them to. Well, we want them to. I won’t precondition the meeting in September other than to say that we raise these issues every time, and we raise it not just – I mean, we raise it all the time. I mean, we raise it through the embassy; we raise it through every engagement we have. Those are always a priority. And we’ve had good news in the past, and hope to have some good news in the future. QUESTION: Secretary — SECRETARY RUBIO: All right, guys. QUESTION: Has Min Zin been recognized as wrongfully detained? He mentioned Min Zin, but has he — SECRETARY RUBIO: Who? QUESTION: Min Zin, who was arrested right after the summit, right after the Trump-Xi summit. SECRETARY RUBIO: The scientist? QUESTION: He – no, not the scientist. He was a researcher, a scholar. SECRETARY RUBIO: Yeah, the researcher, geologist. QUESTION: Not geologist. He was researching for Myanmar, and he was arrested in Yunnan province. But has he been classified as wrongfully detained by the State Department? SECRETARY RUBIO: I don’t believe so yet. QUESTION: Okay. SECRETARY RUBIO: But again, we have a process we go through to make those determinations. That doesn’t mean he won’t be. We just – that process has to work its way through. QUESTION: What is the overall approach, Secretary, to Myanmar and to potentially re-engaging with the junta there or cooperating on issues like rare earths? SECRETARY RUBIO: What’s the — QUESTION: The position or the approach of the Trump Administration towards Myanmar and re-engagement with the government there? SECRETARY RUBIO: Yeah, no – well, I don’t have any announcement for you on that today. It’s a policy that we’re still developing in many ways. Obviously, there’s some conditions that have been shifting with regards to Myanmar or Burma over the last few months that we’re keeping an eye on and see if there’s opportunities to engage. Obviously, we still have many concerns about some of the things that have happened in that country historically in the past. And there also remains the question of how receptive and open they are to a different relationship with the United States as well. So these things are still being worked on, but I don’t have any announcement on that today other than they were here and they were present today. And I’m glad they were here, and I said that in our forum. But it’s not a place we have a long history of engagement in recent times. So if an opportunity presents itself to do something that serves our national interest, we’ll explore it. But there’s still some work to be done in that regard. Okay, guys. Thanks. QUESTION: Just – can you confirm that the White House will be announcing a nuclear deal with Saudi Arabia today? SECRETARY RUBIO: I don’t have any news for you on that today. But maybe later today, once Washington wakes up or – if there is an announcement, I promise you you’ll know about it, okay? QUESTION: Thank you. QUESTION: Thank you. SECRETARY RUBIO: That way. QUESTION: Thank you, sir. title: State Department Establishes Task Force to End Birth Tourism
text: hide State Department Establishes Task Force to End Birth Tourism Fact Sheet Office of the Spokesman August 12, 2026 Under President Trump and Secretary Rubio’s leadership, the Department of State is using all available tools to defend the integrity of U.S. citizenship, ensure nonimmigrant visas are used only for their lawful and intended purposes, and prevent their exploitation through birth tourism. As President Trump has made clear, citizenship is not a commodity to be acquired through the calculated exploitation of U.S. immigration laws. The Department of State is working closely with the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to combat birth tourism and protect the integrity of the U.S. immigration system. New Birth Tourism Prevention Task Force To maximize the success of this comprehensive effort, the State Department has established a Birth Tourism Prevention Task Force. The Birth Tourism Prevention Task Force reviews the activities of visa holders worldwide to identify instances of birth tourism, take action to revoke visas of those who engage in or facilitate it, and dismantle the networks that profit from this abuse. The Task Force addresses the abuse by analyzing and connecting information held across the Department and other federal agencies, including the DHS. Thanks to the coordination of the Task Force, the Department of State is addressing birth tourism on a global scale, examining travel histories of individuals from all around the world in order to end this exploitation and abuse. The Birth Tourism taskforce has taken action by revoking more than 600 visas from foreign nationals across the globe to safeguard our nation from this abuse. The Department generally revokes visas when there are indications of a potential ineligibility. The Secretary has broad discretionary authority to revoke visas – and the Trump Administration is committed to exercising that authority to protect the American people and the integrity of our immigration system. Birth Tourism Has Become a For-Profit Industry Facilitators have turned birth tourism into a lucrative, for-profit industry. These facilitators sometimes market themselves as doulas, midwives, or wellness advocates while openly advertising “birth in the U.S.” services, visa coaching, and hospital arrangements. Some forge medical documents or coach clients to conceal their true travel purpose and avoid paying hospital bills, with online marketing promising clients “automatic citizenship” and “a future without borders.” The facts are clear – birth tourism is a pervasive practice that involves nationals from countries spanning every region of the globe. The Department is taking action to dismantle these networks and hold all participants accountable. Birth Tourism Fraud The work of the Bureau of Consular Affairs Task Force and consular officers at U.S. embassies and consulates around the world is exposing widespread patterns of deception. Foreigners who willfully misrepresent the purpose of their travel or entry into the United States may be permanently ineligible for a U.S. visa or entry to the United States. The Department has uncovered patterns that illustrate the lengths some applicants will go to circumvent our laws in order to secure U.S. citizenship for their children – and potentially for themselves in the future. One couple used a conference and a vacation trip to go shopping as cover stories to give birth to two children in the United States, lying about their travel purpose in two separate visa applications. On the second occasion, the couple concealed that they had a child. The visas have been revoked. In another case, a foreign government official requested a visa to travel on behalf of her government for just one week, but instead stayed three months and gave birth in the United States before departing. The Department revoked the visa. Another traveler applied for a visa to go on vacation in Orlando and instead traveled to Los Angeles and gave birth five days after arrival. The Department revoked the visa. Citizenship is not a commodity to be acquired through calculated exploitation and evasion of the immigration laws. Foreign nationals who abuse the visa system, and those who help them do so, may lose their visa, their access, and their future in the United States. This is only the beginning. title: United States Mobilizes Life-Saving Response to Colombia Earthquake
text: hide United States Mobilizes Life-Saving Response to Colombia Earthquake Media Note Office of the Spokesman August 11, 2026 The Trump Administration has mobilized an immediate response following the devastating 7.4 magnitude earthquake that struck regions of Colombia on August 10. Within hours of the earthquake, the Department of State announced $15.5 million in life-saving emergency shelter, food, and protection assistance, in addition to post-earthquake structural assessments. The Department also activated a Disaster Assistance Response Team (DART), which includes humanitarian experts from across the State Department. Members of the DART began arriving in Colombia the day of this devastating earthquake, underscoring the Department’s commitment to immediate, life-saving action in the critical hours following natural disasters in our hemisphere. The State Department continues to liaise with Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella and the Colombian government as it assesses the impacts of and responds to this earthquake. Disaster Assistance Response Team Deployment The Department is deploying a DART to provide world-class disaster response expertise, technical and programmatic support, operational leadership, and on-the-ground coordination. The DART is responsible for assessing conditions, identifying humanitarian needs, and leading the U.S. Government’s disaster response. The DART is working closely with existing Department assistance personnel, as well as diplomats at our Embassy in Bogota to coordinate with local authorities and partner organizations. Life-Saving Humanitarian Assistance Through Trusted Partners In response to the earthquake, the State Department is mobilizing an initial $15.5 million in life-saving emergency shelter, food, and protection assistance, in addition to post-earthquake structural assessments through trusted partners, including Catholic Relief Services (CRS), the International Organization for Migration, Miyamoto International, the UN World Food Program, and World Vision. Of the $15.5 million in life-saving assistance, $3 million provided through CRS draws from the previously announced CRS global assistance award . With funding already on hand through its global award, CRS can respond immediately through support from the State Department. Additionally, as part of the Department’s $3.8 billion contribution to the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), the United States provided $200 million to the Colombia Pooled Fund, which OCHA can use to address earthquake-related needs as well as preexisting humanitarian needs in Colombia. Supporting Americans in Colombia The Trump Administration has no higher priority than the safety and security of Americans. The Department of State is working tirelessly to provide consular assistance to U.S. citizens and their families in the affected areas. Americans in Colombia should enroll in the Smart Traveler Enrollment Program (STEP) at STEP.state.gov to receive safety and security updates from the U.S. Embassy. They should follow @TravelGov and @USEmbassyBogota on social media for the latest information. The U.S. State Department’s Bureau of Consular Affairs maintains a call center for Americans seeking information or assistance in connection with the Colombia earthquake: call from within the United States 888-407-4747, or from all other locations +1 202-501-4444. title: Mali National Day
text: hide Mali National Day Press Statement Marco Rubio, Secretary of State September 22, 2026 On behalf of the United States of America, I extend warm wishes to the people of Mali as they mark the 66th anniversary of their independence. The United States values its longstanding partnership with Mali and looks forward to deepening ties in the years ahead. We see meaningful opportunities to expand trade and investment that create mutual benefit. American businesses are eager to explore partnerships in sectors where Mali’s resources and talent can drive prosperity. We are deeply cognizant of the security challenges that the government and people of Mali are facing. title: Imposing Sanctions on China- and Iran-based Entities and Individuals that Support Iran’s Ballistic Missile Program
text: hide Imposing Sanctions on China- and Iran-based Entities and Individuals that Support Iran’s Ballistic Missile Program Press Statement Tammy Bruce, Department Spokesperson May 14, 2025 Today, the United States is sanctioning entities and individuals primarily based in China and Hong Kong for their support to Iran’s ballistic missile program. Iran remains heavily reliant on China to conduct its malign activities in the Middle East. This is another example of how the CCP and China-based companies provide key economic and technical support to Iran and its proxies driving regional instability and threatening U.S. partners and allies. Specifically, these entities and individuals are supporting Iran’s efforts to indigenize the manufacturing of carbon fiber for use in Iran’s ballistic missile program. These entities and individuals support the supply of carbon fiber, its precursors, and carbon fiber manufacturing equipment to the various Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) sub-organizations that oversee this effort, including U.S.-designated IRGC Aerospace Force Research and Self Sufficiency Jihad Organization (IRGC ASF RSSJO) and IRGC Research and Self Sufficiency Jehad Organization (IRGC RSSJO). Today’s action is part of President Trump’s National Security Presidential Memorandum-2, which employs maximum pressure to curtail Iran’s ballistic missile program and disrupt, degrade, and deny the IRGC and its terrorist proxies the resources necessary to sustain their destabilizing activities. The United States will use all available means, including sanctions on entities based in third countries, to expose and disrupt Iran’s schemes to procure equipment and items supporting its ballistic missile program, which destabilizes the Middle East and beyond. The Department of Treasury’s action was taken pursuant to Executive Order (E.O.) 13382, which targets proliferators of weapons of mass destruction (WMD) and their supporters. title: United States Sanctioning Iran’s Mahan Air Network and IRGC-Linked Front Company
text: hide United States Sanctioning Iran’s Mahan Air Network and IRGC-Linked Front Company Press Statement Thomas "Tommy" Pigott, Spokesperson July 30, 2026 The United States today sanctioned six entities and individuals in China, India, Russia, and Iran that enable the Iranian regime’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). These include entities that support Mahan Air, the IRGC’s airline of choice for moving weapons, military personnel, and equipment. Today’s action also targets DadeNegar Startup Studio, an IRGC-affiliated front company supporting Iranian military targeting by soliciting locations of American and Israeli equipment in the Middle East. The United States calls on the international community, particularly companies and individuals doing business with Mahan Air or any other sanctioned Iranian carrier, to recognize the serious risks raised by continuing such engagement. The United States will continue to expose and disrupt entities providing the IRGC with the tools and information it uses to threaten American personnel, our partners, and regional stability. OFAC is taking this action pursuant to Executive Order (E.O.) 13224, as amended, which targets terrorist groups, their supporters, and those who aid acts of terrorism, and in furtherance of the President’s National Security Presidential Memorandum 2 (NSPM-2), which directs the U.S. government to deny the IRGC access to assets and resources that sustain its destabilizing activities. On October 12, 2011, OFAC designated Mahan Air pursuant to E.O. 13224 for providing financial, material, and technological support to Iran’s IRGC-Qods Force (IRGC-QF), which OFAC designated pursuant to E.O. 13224 in October 2007 for providing material support to multiple terrorist organizations. The U.S. Department of State designated the IRGC itself pursuant to the counterproliferation authority E.O. 13382 in 2007, and OFAC designated the IRGC pursuant to E.O. 13224 in October 2017 for providing support to the IRGC-QF. F or more information on today’s action, please see Treasury’s press release .
